author: wonder-full
final_message:
All three versions are done and pass every sample.

**Algorithm.** One shortest-path run per source on the undirected graph, exploiting integer weights in 1..1000. Self-loops are dropped. Duplicate sources are computed once and reused. Per source, `R`/`TOTAL`/`FAR`/`NODE` are accumulated as nodes are finalized in increasing distance order (or computed from the final distance array in the NumPy version).

**[Rust](D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder-full/routes/rust/src/main.rs).** Hand-written byte scanner for parsing, CSR adjacency with edges packed into `u64` (neighbor + weight), and Dial's algorithm: a circular bucket array of size `max_w+1` with a bitmap to jump straight to the next non-empty distance level, so no heap and no scanning of empty levels. Distances/buckets/done-stamps are reused across sources. Release profile uses fat LTO, one codegen unit, `panic="abort"` in [Cargo.toml](D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder-full/routes/rust/Cargo.toml). Built offline successfully.

**[plain.py](D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder-full/routes/plain.py).** Same Dial design in pure Python: `map(int, data.split())` into an `array('i')`, CSR as Python lists with each directed edge packed into one int (`neighbor << shift | w`), buckets as lists used as stacks, and a Python-int bitmask to skip empty buckets. The hot loop uses local aliases and iterates adjacency via list slicing.

**[fast.py](D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder-full/routes/fast.py).** NumPy Δ-stepping with all sources batched into one state space (`q*N + node`): vectorized CSR build (bincount/cumsum/argsort), vectorized CSR range expansion for frontier edges, `np.minimum.at` for relaxations, Δ = 1000 (tuned; with weights ≤ 1000 there are no heavy edges). Parsing uses `np.array(data.split(), dtype=np.int64)`, about 4× faster than `np.fromstring` here. If the frontier turns out extremely narrow (e.g. a long path), it falls back to the scalar Dial loop so it cannot degenerate.

**Verification.** All three match `samples/s1–s3` byte-for-byte (modulo line endings). All three also passed 40 randomized tests against an independent `heapq` oracle (disconnected graphs, self-loops, parallel edges, duplicate sources, `M=0`, `N=1`, weight-1000 path): 0 failures. Outputs also agreed across all three on two self-generated 300k-node/900k-edge inputs. Indicative single-run times on those (machine was busy, so noisy): Rust 0.4–0.8 s, fast.py 2.5–3.9 s, plain.py 9.5–14.9 s.

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
